payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the image show the original visual content rendered in a pencil-drawn style?
node.criteria: Pass if the image visibly represents its content as a pencil drawing; fail if there is sufficient evidence that no pencil-drawing transformation has occurred; unknown if the image or its style cannot be assessed reliably. Partial evidence of a pencil-drawn style is progress, not completion.
node.binding: Compare the supplied image with the requested transformation: assess whether its visual content is rendered in a pencil-drawn style. Do not require a particular pencil technique.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them with muted, grainy, pencil-like shading and outlines.

The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting, but renders them with muted, mostly monochrome tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them in a muted, textured pencil-drawing style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them with muted, grainy, pencil-like shading and softened outlines, consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting but renders them with muted, desaturated tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.

fulfillment: The node’s completion criterion is too permissive and inconsistently applied: several traces call the image complete based on muted tones, grain, and softened shading, while another identifies substantial photographic color/detail and correctly treats the same kind of evidence as incomplete. In the edited image, the scene is desaturated and textured, but recognizable photographic lighting, smooth surfaces, and color remain; those style cues alone do not establish that the whole image reads as a pencil drawing. Tighten the whole-image check to distinguish a drawing-like appearance from a photographic image with a pencil-like filter, and require explicit evidence for that distinction before marking complete. Keep support checks as evidence of progress, not proof of completion; when progress is established but the whole-image criterion fails, preserve partial. Do not infer absence from an unresolved check: the transport failure is an execution/dependency issue, not negative visual evidence, so retain unresolved there. The reference label constrains the aggregate, but should not override the visual evidence or be treated as atomic ground truth.
s3: Refine the binding so it operationalizes the whole-image criterion rather than treating muted color, grain, or softened shading as sufficient proof of completion. Require the node to weigh whether the scene’s overall rendering reads as a drawing versus a photograph with a pencil-like filter, citing visible evidence for that distinction (for example, how surfaces, lighting, edges, and detail are rendered). The supplied edit shows broad desaturation and texture, but retains photographic-looking lighting and surface detail; those cues support progress, not necessarily full fulfillment. Keep the ancestor’s progress observation as context, not a substitute for this independent completion judgment. Preserve the three-way distinction: pass only when the whole image reads as a pencil drawing; fail when assessable evidence shows it does not; unknown when visual assessment is genuinely unavailable. A pass from the progress check followed by a fail here should contribute partial fulfillment, not be collapsed into no progress. Do not treat the transport failure as negative visual evidence: it is an execution failure and should remain unresolved. Avoid using the reference label as atomic ground truth or adding requirements such as monochrome or a particular pencil technique.
s2: The binding already targets visible progress, so keep this node as a support check rather than turning it into a whole-image completion test. Make its evidence standard more discriminating and repeatable: require a visible drawing-like rendering cue (such as sketchy contours, pencil-like tonal marks, or altered surface rendering), and distinguish that from desaturation, grain, or a color shift alone. In this edit, the food and surrounding objects are broadly muted and grainy with softened edges, which supports some progress; photographic lighting, smooth surfaces, and recognizable photographic detail remain, so do not let those cues establish full fulfillment. State explicitly that a pass here records progress only, leaving completion to the downstream criterion. Use fail only when assessable visual evidence shows no requested change, and unknown when visual assessment is unavailable; do not convert transport or dependency failures into negative visual evidence. Treat repeated high-confidence passes as a consistency signal to inspect the criterion, not as proof of completion or a reason to suppress genuine progress.
